statements.venue: Weekly column published as a press release on his Senate site
statements.quote: Simply put, if we do not win the AI race, China will – directly threatening our national security.
statements.context: A column arguing the United States must stay ahead of China in AI and regulate it lightly.
statements.reason: The threat named is China winning the AI race, which the rubric treats as competition with China, not catastrophic risk from AI itself.

statements.venue: Weekly column published as a press release on his Senate site
statements.quote: Any government regulations on AI must begin with a “light touch” so that innovators can experiment, prototype, and compete.
statements.context: The same column, setting out his view of how government should regulate AI.
statements.reason: Opposing heavy regulation is not a dismissal of catastrophic risk, and the column names only privacy, jobs and deepfakes as concerns.

statements.venue: Weekly column published as a press release on his Senate site
statements.quote: America must beat China in the artificial intelligence race, and we can do so without letting data centers harm our communities.
statements.context: A column on data centers, electricity bills and the Ratepayer Protection Act.
statements.reason: About the AI race with China and local effects of data centers, with no mention of catastrophic risk from AI.

slowdown.note: No statement found for or against slowing frontier AI development for safety reasons. His calls for 'light touch' regulation and winning the AI race do not address a slowdown directly.

pause.note: No statement found for or against a pause on frontier AI development.

intl.note: No statement found on an agreement or talks with China about the pace of AI development. No source shows him signing the 23 September 2026 letter, which news reports describe as from 17 Democratic senators.

rsi.note: No statement found on a ban on self-improving AI.

record: Signed a letter with Sen. Pete Ricketts and colleagues urging the Commerce Department to withdraw and replace the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule on chip exports.
Introduced, with Sen. Peter Welch and Rep. Harriet Hageman, a bill to set up a task force studying AI speech-to-text tools in federal courts.
As Armed Services chairman, agreed to include Sen. Tom Cotton's chip-tracking bill in the managers' amendment to the fiscal 2027 defense authorization bill, according to Roll Call.
grade_reason: The missing search on the defense bill found no remarks from him on catastrophic AI risk. His recorded AI remarks are still about beating China, light regulation and data centers.
notes: Only 8 of the intended searches ran; a ninth (on the defense bill and advanced AI) was blocked by the session search limit, so hearing remarks and floor speeches as Armed Services chairman were not searched specifically. The three quotes were checked by script as exact substrings of the live Senate pages. The May 2025 column also says "In the U.S. Senate, my colleagues and I are working to balance the risks and rewards of AI." but the risks it names are privacy, jobs and deepfakes, so it stays at D. 23 September 2026 China letter: reports (KMPH/Sinclair, Morung Express) describe 17 Democratic senators led by Chris Van Hollen; I did not find the full signer list, and nothing shows Wicker signed. Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: sources name only Sen. Sanders and House Democrats; I did not check congress.gov, and nothing shows Wicker co-sponsored. Left out as not his words: a Yahoo/NBC report of 19 November 2025 says he 'declined to comment' on putting a moratorium on state AI laws into the defense bill. The Hageman press release and the April 2025 letter release were seen in search results only, not opened; the Roll Call article was opened through a summarising fetch tool. A search summary claimed he co-sponsored the Cantwell-Young Future of AI Innovation Act and the 2023 AI Research, Innovation, and Accountability Act; both predate 2025 and were not verified, so they are not in the record. March 2026 date for the courts bill comes from a search summary (19 March 2026), not verified at source. Searches rerun on 15 November 2026: 2 ran, none refused; 0 new statements. Notes from the rerun: Only one search had not run (the defense-bill search); it was run now, plus one follow-up on hearing remarks. Neither was refused. The six required topics were already covered by the earlier run, so they were not repeated. Opened the Armed Services Committee press release on completing the fiscal 2027 defense bill markup (https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/press-releases/sasc-completes-markup-of-national-defense-authorization-act-for-fiscal-year-2027) through a summarising fetch tool; its only AI line attributed to Wicker is "The bill responds to the modern battlefield with thoughtful approaches on artificial intelligence" (as returned by the tool, possibly shortened; the sentence also mentions autonomous weapons, munitions and cyber operations). That is a passing, military-use mention (level D at most) and less substantial than the D statements already in the file, so it is left out. News coverage says the committee's bill requires human oversight of AI-enabled weapons and lists a Defense Department provision on AI risk governance, but these are committee provisions, not his words, and military use is D under ruling 3; not added to the record. A June 2026 letter from outside groups to Wicker and others urged AI safeguards in the bill; that is a letter to him, not by him. The follow-up search found 2026 Senate hearings on rogue AI agents and superintelligence risk (Homeland Security 30 Sept, Hawley hearing 1 Oct, HELP 1 May), but no source showing Wicker spoke at them. Wicker is not on the verified signer list of the 23 September 2026 China letter.
